title: What to Say When a Stakeholder Wants to Add "Just One More Thing"
author: Workshop Bank
summary: Workshop Bank offers facilitators a repeatable three-move script for handling last-minute stakeholder scope creep: never say no outright, name the trade-off the addition actually costs, and hand the decision back to the person who raised it. The newsletter walks through five common requests -- adding a topic, adding attendees, extending the session length, giving a senior leader unstructured airtime, and adding a second objective -- with a specific line for each that makes the hidden cost visible rather than absorbing it silently. Its underlying claim is that a workshop is a fixed container of attention and time, so every addition displaces something else, and stakeholders routinely can't see that trade-off until a facilitator names it in concrete terms (which outcome gets cut, what happens above twelve participants, what an unscripted CEO welcome tends to do to an agenda). The piece reframes the facilitator's job not as gatekeeping against the client but as making costs visible so the client can protect their own original design, closing with a worked real-engagement example showing all three requests handled in under five minutes each.
points: The core three-step script -- never say no outright, name the trade-off, hand the decision back to the stakeholder -- reframes scope-creep pushback from an adversarial refusal into a service that makes an invisible cost visible.

For added participants specifically, the piece gives a concrete design ceiling: above twelve people, a discussion-based workshop format breaks down into something closer to a presentation, with far less depth and airtime per person.

Its "one-outcome-per-hour" rule holds that two real objectives packed into one half-day session produce two half-baked results rather than one that actually changes behavior, so competing objectives should be split into separate sessions rather than compressed together.

For senior leaders asked to "say a few words," the recommended fix is a tight two-minute brief focused on personal stakes rather than an unscripted welcome, on the theory that most executives prefer clear constraints to open-ended improvisation.
quotes: But every yes has a cost the stakeholder can't see. They think facilitation is elastic, that a session can stretch to hold whatever you pour into it. It can't.
A workshop is a designed thing with a fixed amount of attention, energy, and time to work with. Add to one part and another part gives way.

Asking them to name what they'd drop makes the cost concrete. The addition has a price. Two things happen when you ask this. The stakeholder realises the original plan was more considered than they assumed.
A workshop built for eight runs on pair conversations, individual writing, and full-group shares where everyone gets airtime. Put twenty-two people into that same design and it breaks.

This is the one-outcome-per-hour rule I bang on about. Two real objectives in a half-day session means neither gets the depth to change anything. You split the time, and you produce two half-baked results and neither one sticks.
You're not the gatekeeper protecting your design from the client. You're the guide showing the client what their own design costs, so they can choose to protect it themselves.
